html-entities-encoder-decoder.assumptionNote: Encoding is lossless and reversible; decoding unknown entities leaves them unchanged.
benefits: Display raw HTML code on a page without the browser rendering it.
Basic mode escapes only the five dangerous characters; Full mode also covers Unicode.
Decoder handles named, decimal, and hex entities — including emoji code points.
Live conversion with character counts shows exactly what changed.
One click copies the result for pasting into code or CMS editors.

faqs.a: Switch to the Encode tab, choose Basic scope, paste your HTML, and copy the output. Paste the encoded text where the code should display as text — for example inside a <pre> block.
faqs.q: How do I show HTML code as text on my page?

faqs.a: The five characters are & < > " and '. They are the only ones that can break HTML parsing or enable script injection, so escaping them is enough for safe display.
faqs.q: Which five characters does Basic mode escape?

faqs.a: Full mode additionally converts every character above code point 127 — accented letters, symbols, emoji — into &#x...; entities. Use it when your page encoding is uncertain or you need pure ASCII output.
faqs.q: When should I use Full mode instead of Basic?

faqs.a: Switch to the Decode tab and paste the entity text. Named entities like ©, decimal like ©, and hex like © are all converted back.
faqs.q: How do I convert entities back to normal text?

faqs.a: Unknown entities are left unchanged so nothing is lost. Only recognized named entities (a built-in list of common ones) plus numeric forms are decoded.
faqs.q: What happens to entities the decoder does not know?

faqs.a: Yes — decoding is the exact inverse for anything this tool encoded, and numeric entities always round-trip. Named entities decode if they are in the built-in list.

howTo: Choose the Encode or Decode tab.
For encoding, pick Basic or Full scope.
Paste your text into the input box.
Copy the result with the copy button.
keyFacts: HTML entities let you write reserved characters as text, like < for <.
The five reserved characters are & < > " and '.
Numeric entities use character codes: © and © both mean ©.
Named entities like © are easier to read but fewer are standardized.
Browsers decode entities when parsing HTML into the DOM.
html-entities-encoder-decoder.keywords: html entities encoder, html escape online, unescape html, html entity decoder, encode html special chars
limitations: The decoder knows common named entities; rare ones are left as-is.
Encoding does not sanitize JavaScript — it only escapes markup characters.
Full mode output is verbose; prefer Basic unless you need ASCII-only text.
Decoding cannot recover text from double-encoded entities in one pass.

html-entities-encoder-decoder.quickAnswer: Browsers treat < and > as markup, so showing raw HTML as text requires escaping them as entities like <. This tool converts text to entities (encode) and entities back to text (decode), with a basic mode for the five reserved characters and a full mode that also encodes Unicode.
html-entities-encoder-decoder.tagline: Escape HTML special characters — or decode entities back.
html-entities-encoder-decoder.workedExample:
Encode A&B in Basic mode. < becomes <, " becomes ", > becomes >, & becomes &. Output: <a href="x">A&B</a> Paste that into a
